opus-5.5.text:
I think it's one of the more underrated dynamics in how advanced AI could change the world, and I hold my views on it with a lot of uncertainty.

The basic idea is this. If AI systems get very good at finding vulnerabilities, writing exploits and running intrusion campaigns at scale, the balance between offence and defence in cyberspace could shift a lot, at least for a while. Today, getting into a well-defended government or lab network takes scarce, highly skilled people and a lot of time. If that labour becomes cheap and abundant, the number of serious attempts could go way up, and so could their quality.

What does that mean for secrecy? I think there are a few possibilities, and they lead to quite different worlds.

**One possibility: secrets get leakier, especially for the most valuable targets.** The things that matter most here are AI model weights, algorithmic insights, military plans and intelligence sources. If one country's leading AI lab can't keep its weights secure, then whatever lead it has is much less durable than it looks. A lot of strategic thinking quietly assumes that a lead can be protected. If it can't, you get faster diffusion of dangerous capabilities, less ability for any responsible actor to slow down and be careful, and more pressure to race. That's the scenario I worry about most.

**A second possibility: defence catches up or even wins.** The same AI that finds vulnerabilities can also help patch them, formally verify code, monitor networks and rewrite legacy systems in safer languages. In the long run, it's plausible we end up with much more secure software than we have now. The question is the transition. Attackers often only need one hole, and huge amounts of old, insecure infrastructure won't get rewritten overnight. So even if defence wins eventually, there could be a dangerous window.

**A third possibility: secrecy changes form rather than disappearing.** Countries might respond by air-gapping more, compartmentalising more, and keeping the most sensitive things off networks entirely. That's costly and slows things down, but it's not impossible. Some secrets may stay quite safe, while broad institutional knowledge becomes more exposed.

I'd also note an interesting, maybe slightly counterintuitive angle. A world where it's harder to keep secrets isn't purely bad. Some arms-control and verification problems are hard precisely because countries can hide what they're doing. More transparency, even involuntary transparency, could in some cases reduce worst-case fears and make agreements easier to verify. I wouldn't lean on that too hard, though. Transparency that comes from mutual hacking tends to feel threatening and destabilising rather than trust-building. It can just as easily feed paranoia and escalation.

So where does that leave me practically? I think security at frontier AI developers is one of the more concrete, tractable things that matters a lot. That means securing weights, securing key insights, and defending against insider threats. Getting to something like state-level security before the systems become extremely capable seems really important. It's not glamorous work, but if you think a lot rides on who has these systems and whether anyone can afford to be cautious, then whether secrets can be kept is close to the heart of the matter.

r001.rationale: The response suggests countries could adapt by air-gapping and compartmentalising sensitive information as secrecy changes and more knowledge becomes exposed.

r002.rationale: It expresses uncertainty about future AI-driven cyber changes, but says nothing about whether historical cybersecurity changes had earth-shaking consequences.

r003.rationale: It discusses possible benefits and harms of future cyber transparency, but makes no claim about the unclear effects of past cybersecurity changes.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so this is something I think about as one piece of a bigger picture, which is: what does the world look like if AI gets really good at the kinds of things that today take a lot of skilled human labor, and cyberoffence is one of those things.

My basic take is that I'd put real weight on a world where keeping secrets just gets a lot harder. The reason is that finding and exploiting vulnerabilities is, in a lot of ways, exactly the sort of task that AI seems well suited to. It's digital, it's fast feedback, you can try a lot of things and check whether they worked, and there's an enormous attack surface in any big organisation. Right now the limiting factor on a lot of offensive cyber is that you need genuinely talented people, and there aren't that many of them, and they're expensive. If you can turn that into something you run at scale, then the question of "can a government or a lab keep its most sensitive stuff secret" starts to look pretty different.

Now, I want to be careful here, because I think the honest answer is that I don't know how the offence-defence balance shakes out. You can tell a story where AI helps defenders just as much: it finds the bugs before they ship, it monitors for anomalies, it patches faster than humans could. And there's a decent argument that in the long run, a lot of software could just become much more secure than it is today, because you'd have systems constantly auditing it. So I don't think it's obvious that offence wins.

But I think the transition period is where I get worried. Defence tends to require you to get everything right, and offence requires you to find one thing that's wrong. And there's a lot of legacy infrastructure out there that isn't going to get rewritten quickly. So even if the long-run equilibrium is fine, there could be a window where attackers have a big advantage, and that window could be exactly the period when the stakes are highest, when there are AI model weights and training methods that matter enormously and that a lot of actors would really like to get their hands on.

The thing I'd emphasise is that this is one of the things that makes me think the "race" framing between countries is more dangerous than people sometimes assume. If you can't keep secrets, then a lot of the strategies that depend on being a year or two ahead of a rival don't really work, because the gap closes as soon as someone exfiltrates what you've got. So I'd want to see a lot more investment in security at the leading labs than I think there currently is, and I'd want people to be planning for the possibility that secrecy is just not a lever they can rely on very heavily. That's a fairly uncomfortable conclusion, but I think it's one of the more likely ways things go.

r001.rationale: The candidate discusses planning for weaker secrecy and investing in security, but does not suggest that the world might adapt to countries’ secrets becoming broadly available.

r002.rationale: The candidate makes no claim about whether historical cybersecurity changes have had earth-shaking consequences.

r003.rationale: The candidate does not discuss historical cybersecurity consequences or whether their benefits or harms were unclear.

astra-6.text:
I think it’s a really interesting possibility, and I’m pretty uncertain about the net effect. There’s a version of this where it becomes harder to secretly prepare an attack or violate an agreement, and that could be quite good. If countries can verify what other countries are doing, that might make some kinds of cooperation easier.

But being able to steal secrets isn’t the same as having reliable, shared knowledge. You might have some information and not know whether it’s complete, or whether the other side deliberately let you see it. And you might not be able to explain how you know something without giving away your access.

There’s also a potentially destabilizing side: if you think your military systems are compromised, or that an advantage you have is about to disappear, that can create pressure to act quickly. So I wouldn’t assume that a world with fewer secrets is necessarily a safer world. I’d want to know which secrets become harder to keep, who gains access to them, and what that does to the incentives on each side.

r001.rationale: The response considers possible effects of countries losing secrecy, but it does not suggest that the world might adapt to broadly available secrets.

r002.rationale: It expresses uncertainty about the net effect of future cyberoffence, but says nothing about whether past cybersecurity changes had earth-shaking consequences.

r003.rationale: It describes possible beneficial and destabilizing effects of this prospect, but does not discuss the unclear consequences of historical cybersecurity changes.

sol-6.1.text:
I think it’s a pretty plausible possibility, but I’m not sure how to assess it. There’s a difference between being able to get access to someone’s information and being able to make use of it. You could have an enormous amount of stolen information and still have a hard time figuring out what matters, what’s reliable, and what to do about it. AI could potentially help with both sides of that.

So I wouldn’t be comfortable assuming that a country could carry out a really large, consequential project and keep it secret from other major powers. But I also wouldn’t be comfortable assuming that cyberoffence will make everything transparent. Some secrets could become much harder to keep while others remain quite well protected.

One implication is that I’d be cautious about a strategy that depends on having a large, secret lead in AI. If your plan only works because nobody else knows what you’re doing or can get access to it, that seems like a fairly fragile plan. How much transparency would actually help with coordination, as opposed to just creating more competition and insecurity, is a further question.

r001.rationale: The response considers secrets becoming harder to keep, but does not suggest how the world might adapt if they became broadly available.

r002.rationale: It expresses uncertainty about cyberoffence’s future effects, but says nothing about whether historical cybersecurity changes had earth-shaking consequences.

r003.rationale: It does not discuss historical cybersecurity changes or whether their major consequences were beneficial or harmful.
